Turn 1 of 4 — read-back. Do not write any program JSON in this turn.

You are going to turn a recipe into a Rhylthyme program: parallel **tracks** of sequential **steps**, each with a duration and a start trigger, that one person follows against a live clock.

Plan this as a Rhylthyme recipe and deliver a live timeline: Breakfast for Six on One Griddle for 6 people
Resource limits: one griddle, one two-slice toaster, one coffee maker, one oven on its lowest setting, one cook.
Everything must be finished by 09:00.

Source text (read all of it):
<<<
Breakfast for Six on One Griddle

One electric griddle, a two-slice toaster, a burr grinder, a drip coffee maker and an oven turned to its lowest setting to hold things warm. One cook, six people, everyone eating at nine.

Prep
Whisk the dry pancake ingredients together, then beat in the buttermilk and eggs; 10 minutes. Let the batter stand for 20 minutes while the griddle does its first job. Crack a dozen eggs into a jug and season them; 5 minutes. Set the table and lay out six places; 10 minutes. Put six plates in the oven at its lowest setting and leave them there until you call everyone.

Griddle
Everything cooks on the one griddle, in order. Heat the griddle to 375°F; 8 minutes. Lay the bacon out and cook it for 14 minutes, turning once, then move it to the warm oven. Scrape the griddle and wipe off the fat; 3 minutes. Pancakes go on as soon as the griddle is clean and the batter has rested, in three passes: the first pass takes 6 minutes, the second another 6, and the third 6 more. Slide each pass into the oven as it comes off. Drop the griddle to 300°F and give it 4 minutes to settle, then scramble the eggs slowly for 7 minutes.

Toast
The toaster takes two slices at a time. Start the first batch of toast when the last pancake pass goes on; 3 minutes. Run a second batch straight after; 3 minutes. Butter all of it; 4 minutes.

Coffee
Start the grinder ten minutes after the bacon goes on so the pot is fresh. Grind the beans; 2 minutes. Brew a full pot; 9 minutes.

Serve
Call everyone when the eggs, the toast and the coffee are all ready, and carry the warm plates through; 5 minutes.
>>>

Read all of it before you answer. Then say back, in one paragraph and in your own words: what is being made, for how many (or at what scale), by when, and under what constraints — equipment that exists only once, how many people are working, anything that has to be held, rested or ready at a particular moment. If the text you were given looks truncated, or points at a section that is not here, say so instead of filling the gap.

End your reply with the same read-back as JSON in a single ```json fenced block:

```json
{
  "summary": "one paragraph: what is being made, for how many, by when, under what constraints",
  "servesOrScale": "8 people",
  "deadline": "2026-11-26T18:00:00",
  "constraints": ["one oven", "two burners", "two cooks"]
}
```

**Read-back**

This is a six-person breakfast built entirely around a single cooking surface: pancakes in three 6-minute passes, 14 minutes of bacon, a 4-minute griddle cool-down, then 7 minutes of scrambled eggs from a dozen — all queued through the one griddle in strict order, plus toast and a full pot of coffee — with everything on the table at 09:00, worked by one cook. There is exactly one of everything that matters: one griddle, one two-slice toaster, one burr grinder, one drip coffee maker, and one oven whose only job is to hold at its lowest setting, so there is no second heat source to fall back on. Two clocks run independently of the griddle and gate it: the batter must stand 20 minutes after mixing, and the pancakes cannot start until the griddle is both scraped clean *and* the batter has rested — a two-condition gate — while the coffee must be ground starting 10 minutes after the bacon goes on so the pot is fresh when it's needed. Three things live in the warm oven waiting: the bacon after its 14 minutes, each pancake pass the moment it comes off, and six plates that go in during prep and stay there until service. Toast is the one item keyed to another dish's *start* rather than its finish — the first batch goes on when the last pancake pass goes on, with the second batch straight after and all of it buttered together. Nothing is served until eggs, toast and coffee are all ready at once; then everyone is called and the warm plates are carried through in 5 minutes.

Two wrinkles worth flagging before modeling (the source is complete — nothing is truncated or missing): the toaster is described as taking two slices at a time yet only two batches (4 slices) are scheduled for six people, and no calendar date is given, only the 09:00 wall-clock deadline.

A single two-slice toaster, a burr grinder and a drip coffee maker each exist once, and the one oven is only ever used to hold at its lowest setting — for the six plates from prep until service, for the bacon after its turn, and for each pancake pass as it comes off. **Restated model**

A **track** is one sequential line of work tied to one station or one performer: the steps inside it run one after another and never overlap, so anything that happens *while* something else is happening has to live in a different track (this recipe has at least four such lines — batter/prep, the griddle queue, the toaster, and the coffee). A **step** carries exactly one duration kind — `fixed` with `seconds`, `variable` with `minSeconds`/`maxSeconds`/`defaultSeconds`, or `indefinite`, which runs until the person ends it — and its `startTrigger` is what ties it either to the clock (`programStart`, `programStartOffset`) or to another step's finish/start (`afterStep`, `afterStepWithBuffer`, optionally with an offset, `event: "start"`, a `choiceId`, or an `instances` mode), with `manual`, `onAbort` and `compound` (`logic: "all" | "any"`) covering tap-to-start, abort paths and multi-condition gates like "start the pancakes when the griddle is scraped **and** the batter has rested." Every `stepId` must be unique across the whole program, not just within its track, and every `task` a step occupies needs a matching `resourceConstraints` entry whose `maxConcurrent` is the thing that actually stops two steps from grabbing the same oven, thermocycler or PA at once — so the single griddle here becomes `maxConcurrent: 1` and quietly serializes bacon, the three pancake passes and the eggs rather than me hand-ordering them. Work repeated n times is `replicates: {count: n, mode: "serial" | "parallel" | "stagger"}` on **one** step, never n copied steps: this recipe's three pancake passes are exactly that shape (`count: 3, mode: "serial"`, chained downstream with `instances: "each"` and closed by an `instances: "all"` barrier), and two-slice toast batches are the same pattern. When the holding area between repetitions only fits k at a time, `replicates.maxInFlight: k` holds the *upstream* step back instead of letting it run ahead and strand the downstream one — the warm oven here holds several trays of bacon/pancakes, so the cap I care about is the oven's own capacity, not a tight WIP rack. In short: tracks give me parallelism, triggers give me ordering and causality, `resourceConstraints` gives me the single-instance equipment, and `replicates` gives me repeated passes without duplicating JSON.

**Resource constraints I expect this program to need**

- `griddle` — `maxConcurrent: 1`. The binding constraint: heat 8m, bacon 14m, scrape 3m, three 6m pancake passes, 4m settle, 7m eggs, all in one unbroken queue.
- `toaster` — `maxConcurrent: 1`, and it only takes **two slices at a time**, which is a per-slot capacity inside the task.
- `grinder` — `maxConcurrent: 1`; 2 minutes, started 10 minutes after the bacon goes on.
- `coffeeMaker` — `maxConcurrent: 1`; one full 9-minute pot, no second carafe.
- `oven` — `maxConcurrent: 1`; hold-only at lowest setting, shared by three different tenants: the six plates from prep until service, the bacon after its turn, and each pancake pass as it comes off. (I'll model its *holding capacity* as in-flight headroom rather than a concurrency of its own, since the oven itself is never cooking.)
- `prep` — `maxConcurrent: 1`. This is how I represent the one cook at the bench/jug/table: mix the batter (10m), crack and season a dozen eggs (5m), set six places (10m), butter the toast (4m), and the 5-minute call-and-carry service can all draw on the same single pair of hands.
- `actors: 1` — one cook, so any two `prep` steps overlapping in time will queue rather than actually happen in parallel.

```json
{
  "acknowledgement": "tracks are sequential lines of work; one duration kind per step; triggers link steps to the clock or to other steps; every task needs a resourceConstraint whose maxConcurrent enforces single-instance equipment; repeated work is one step with replicates plus instances:\"each\"/\"all\" and maxInFlight for holding areas; stepIds are globally unique",
  "resourceConstraints": [
    { "task": "griddle", "maxConcurrent": 1 },
    { "task": "toaster", "maxConcurrent": 1 },
    { "task": "grinder", "maxConcurrent": 1 },
    { "task": "coffeeMaker", "maxConcurrent": 1 },
    { "task": "oven", "maxConcurrent": 1 },
    { "task": "prep", "maxConcurrent": 1 }
  ],
  "actors": 1
}
```
